Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

CLOVIS, California (CNN) -- Jeff Hubbard fought back tears as he talked about his boy -- a "great, great young man" who was killed last week in Iraq in a helicopter crash. It's the second time he's had to bury a son killed in the Iraq war. Jeff and Peggy Hubbard with sons  Army Spc. Jason Hubbard, left, and Cpl. Nathan Hubbard. This time, it was made even more tragic. His third son, also a soldier in Iraq, was immediately on the scene of last week's helicopter crash and watched as soldiers carried the remains of his brother, 21-year-old Army Cpl. Nathan Hubbard, from the crash site. Nathan's flag-draped coffin arrived in Fresno earlier this week and eventually to his hometown of Clovis.  Watch "We love you Nate" » . Hundreds of mourners gathered Friday to remember Nathan at St. Anthony of Padua, the same church where his oldest brother's funeral was held in 2004. Nathan will be laid to rest at Clovis Cemetery, beside his brother, Jared. Nathan and his other brother entered the military shortly after Jared was killed -- to honor his sacrifice. "Their decision to join the military was motivated by a love for their brother and a desire to serve their country," the priest told mourners Friday. "The death of Jared touched him deeply. Losing a brother and a friend made a profound impact on him, and brought to his attention the seasons of war and grief and loss." Jeff Hubbard spoke to reporters Thursday ahead of the funeral, struggling to find words to describe how much his youngest son meant to him and his family. "I want everybody to remember and celebrate Nate in their own way, the way they want," he said. "We want him honored, remembered and celebrated -- he was a great, great young man. Wonderful young man." Tragically, the Hubbards have gone through this anguish before. In 2004 their son, Marine Lance Cpl. Jared Hubbard, was on patrol in Iraq with his best friend and fellow Marine, Jeremiah Baro -- also from Clovis -- when a roadside bomb exploded, killing both. Jeff Hubbard says there's no way for a parent to prepare for the agony a second time. "They're each absolutely individual terrible instances that you deal with the best you can as you go forward," he said. Six months after Jared was killed, Nathan and Jason Hubbard decided to enlist and serve together -- to follow in their brother's footsteps. On August 22 after returning from a scouting mission south of Kirkuk, Iraq, the Blackhawk helicopter carrying Nathan and 13 other soldiers crashed. Jason, who served in the same Army platoon, was in a separate helicopter when his brother went down and was ordered to secure the crash site. When he and his men reached the downed Blackhawk, Jason says he realized it was his brother's unit. "We also had to remove as many of the men as we could out of that helicopter," Jason remembered. "And I couldn't participate in that. I knew my -- I knew Nathan was in there. I tried several times to kind of gather myself, but I just -- I couldn't." Jason says as the men carried bodies out of the wreckage, he spotted his younger brother. "At one point they did carry Nathan by me. And that's when the reality, the complete reality, and complete understanding of the situation came to me and I began dealing with it." Under the Department of Defense sole survivor policy, Jason says he was told he will not be allowed to return to war. His wife and young son will join him at his base in Hawaii.  E-mail to a friend .

outputs.L1:
**CLOVIS, California (CNN)** — Jeff Hubbard fought back tears as he spoke about his son—a “great, great young man” who was killed last week in a helicopter crash in Iraq. It is the second time he has had to bury a son killed in the Iraq war.

*Jeff and Peggy Hubbard with their sons, Army Spc. Jason Hubbard, left, and Cpl. Nathan Hubbard.*

This time, the tragedy was compounded: His third son, also a soldier in Iraq, was among the first to arrive at the scene of last week’s helicopter crash and watched as soldiers carried the remains of his brother, 21-year-old Army Cpl. Nathan Hubbard, from the site.

Nathan’s flag-draped coffin arrived in Fresno earlier this week and was eventually brought to his hometown of Clovis. *Watch “We love you, Nate” »*

Hundreds of mourners gathered Friday at St. Anthony of Padua to remember Nathan. It was the same church where his oldest brother’s funeral was held in 2004. Nathan will be laid to rest at Clovis Cemetery beside his brother, Jared.

Nathan and his other brother entered the military shortly after Jared was killed, seeking to honor his sacrifice.

“Their decision to join the military was motivated by a love for their brother and a desire to serve their country,” the priest told mourners Friday. “The death of Jared touched him deeply. Losing a brother and a friend made a profound impact on him and brought to his attention the seasons of war and grief and loss.”

Speaking to reporters Thursday ahead of the funeral, Jeff Hubbard struggled to find the words to express how much his youngest son meant to him and his family.

“I want everybody to remember and celebrate Nate in their own way, the way they want,” he said. “We want him honored, remembered and celebrated—he was a great, great young man. Wonderful young man.”

Tragically, the Hubbards have endured this anguish before. In 2004, their son, Marine Lance Cpl. Jared Hubbard, was on patrol in Iraq with his best friend and fellow Marine, Jeremiah Baro—also from Clovis—when a roadside bomb exploded, killing them both.

Jeff Hubbard said there is no way for a parent to prepare for such agony a second time.

“They’re each absolutely individual terrible instances that you deal with the best you can as you go forward,” he said.

Six months after Jared was killed, Nathan and Jason Hubbard decided to enlist and serve together, following in their brother’s footsteps.

On August 22, after returning from a scouting mission south of Kirkuk, Iraq, the Black Hawk helicopter carrying Nathan and 13 other soldiers crashed. Jason, who served in the same Army platoon, was aboard a separate helicopter when his brother’s aircraft went down and was ordered to secure the crash site.

When he and his men reached the downed Black Hawk, Jason said he realized it was his brother’s unit.

“We also had to remove as many of the men as we could out of that helicopter,” Jason recalled. “And I couldn’t participate in that. I knew my—I knew Nathan was in there. I tried several times to kind of gather myself, but I just—I couldn’t.”

Jason said that, as the men carried bodies from the wreckage, he saw his younger brother.

“At one point they did carry Nathan by me. And that’s when the reality, the complete reality, and complete understanding of the situation came to me, and I began dealing with it.”

Under the Department of Defense’s sole-survivor policy, Jason said he was told that he would not be allowed to return to war. His wife and young son will join him at his base in Hawaii.

*E-mail to a friend.*

CLOVIS, California (CNN) — Fighting back tears, Jeff Hubbard described his son Nathan as a “wonderful” young man. The 21-year-old Army corporal died the previous week when a Blackhawk helicopter crashed in Iraq, making him the second Hubbard son to be killed in the war.

The tragedy was compounded by the experience of Jeff and Peggy Hubbard’s surviving son, Army Spc. Jason Hubbard. Also serving in Iraq, Jason arrived at the crash site almost immediately and saw soldiers remove his younger brother’s remains from the wreckage.

Nathan’s coffin, covered with an American flag, reached Fresno earlier in the week before being taken to his hometown of Clovis. Hundreds of people gathered Friday at St. Anthony of Padua to honor him. The same church had hosted the funeral of his oldest brother, Marine Lance Cpl. Jared Hubbard, in 2004. Nathan was to be buried next to Jared at Clovis Cemetery.

Nathan and Jason had enlisted six months after Jared’s death, hoping to honor their brother’s sacrifice by following him into military service. During Friday’s funeral, the priest said their choice reflected both their devotion to Jared and their wish to serve the United States. He added that Jared’s death had affected Nathan profoundly, forcing him to confront war, sorrow and loss after losing both a brother and a friend.

Speaking with reporters on Thursday before the funeral, Jeff struggled to explain what his youngest son had meant to the family. He said people should remember and celebrate Nate in whatever way felt right to them, adding that the family wanted him to be honored and remembered as the “great, great young man” he was.

The Hubbards had endured similar grief three years earlier. In 2004, Jared was patrolling in Iraq with his best friend and fellow Marine, Jeremiah Baro, who was also from Clovis, when a roadside bomb detonated and killed them both.

Jeff said nothing could prepare a parent to suffer such pain for a second time. Each death, he explained, was its own uniquely terrible event, and the family could only cope as best it could while continuing forward.

On August 22, Nathan was among 14 soldiers aboard a Blackhawk returning from a reconnaissance mission south of Kirkuk, Iraq, when the aircraft went down. Jason, a member of the same Army platoon, was traveling in another helicopter. After the crash, he was instructed to secure the area.

When Jason and the soldiers with him reached the wrecked Blackhawk, he recognized that it belonged to his brother’s unit. Their assignment included removing as many men as possible from the aircraft, but Jason said he could not take part because he knew Nathan was inside. Although he repeatedly tried to compose himself, he was unable to do so.

As the bodies were carried from the wreckage, Jason saw his younger brother pass by. He said that moment brought the full reality of what had happened into focus and marked the beginning of his effort to process the loss.

Under the Department of Defense’s sole-survivor policy, Jason said he had been informed that he would not be permitted to return to combat. His wife and young son were expected to join him at his military base in Hawaii.

The original report also included a “We love you Nate” video link and an option to e-mail the story to a friend.

The Hubbard family had already endured the death of one son in Iraq when war claimed another.

Army Cpl. Nathan Hubbard, 21, died in a helicopter crash while serving in Iraq, three years after his brother Jared was killed there. For relatives, friends, fellow soldiers, and members of the family’s community, Nathan’s death reopened an old wound while creating a new one. Their grief was not only for a young man whose life had ended, but also for a family forced to confront the cost of war for a second time.

Accounts from Nathan’s family and those who knew him portray a close-knit household shaped by devotion to one another and by the brothers’ commitment to military service. Jared’s death had already changed the family permanently. Nathan nevertheless continued to serve, carrying both his own sense of duty and the memory of his brother with him.

The tragedy was made still more painful by the presence of a third Hubbard brother serving in Iraq. He encountered the aftermath of the crash in which Nathan died, bringing the loss terrifyingly close. Instead of learning about the death from afar, he was confronted with its immediate reality while still in a combat zone. His experience underscored how deeply the war had entered the family’s life: one brother had been killed, another had now died, and a third was left to witness and survive the consequences.

Back home, news of Nathan’s death spread through a community that remembered mourning Jared only a few years earlier. Friends, neighbors, veterans, and local residents gathered around the Hubbards, offering condolences and trying to comprehend the scale of the family’s sacrifice. The funeral became both a farewell to Nathan and a public expression of shared grief.

Military honors recognized Nathan’s service, but the ceremony also emphasized everything that had been lost. He was remembered not simply as a soldier, but as a son, brother, friend, and young man whose future had been cut short. The presence of mourners from across the community showed that his death extended beyond the immediate family. Teachers, classmates, acquaintances, and strangers alike were affected by the knowledge that the same household had given two sons to the war.

Interviews with the family reveal grief layered upon grief. Memories of Nathan are inseparable from memories of Jared, and the brothers’ deaths are now linked in the family’s history. Yet those recollections also preserve their individuality. Each brother had his own personality, relationships, ambitions, and reasons for serving. Remembering them means resisting the tendency to see them only as symbols of sacrifice.

At the same time, the Hubbard family’s experience has become an especially stark example of the burden carried by military families. War is often described through casualty totals, operations, and distant events. For the Hubbards, it arrived repeatedly and personally: in official notifications, an empty place at home, a funeral, and then the return of the same devastating rituals three years later.

Nathan Hubbard’s death therefore represents more than a single casualty in a helicopter crash. It is the story of a family asked to bear an almost unimaginable loss twice, of a surviving brother marked by what he saw, and of a community once again gathering to bury one of its young people. Through the family’s testimony and the solemn scenes of the funeral, the human consequences of the Iraq War come into focus—not as an abstraction, but as an absence that will remain with the Hubbards and those around them for years to come.

**Clovis family buries second son killed in Iraq as surviving brother recounts recovery mission**

**CLOVIS, Calif. —** Army Spc. Nathan H. Hubbard was laid to rest with full military honors in his hometown after becoming the second son in his family to die while serving in Iraq, a loss made even more painful by the presence of his surviving brother, Jason, at the recovery of Nathan’s remains.

Hubbard, 21, was among 14 U.S. soldiers killed Aug. 22, 2007, when a UH-60 Black Hawk helicopter crashed during a nighttime mission in northern Iraq. The military said hostile fire was not believed to have caused the crash.

At the funeral in Clovis, relatives, friends, fellow soldiers and members of the community gathered to remember a young infantryman who had followed his two older brothers into the Army despite already knowing the cost of war. A flag-draped casket, an honor guard, the playing of taps and a rifle salute marked the formal military farewell.

Nathan was buried near his older brother, Army Cpl. Jared W. Hubbard, 22, who was killed in Mosul, Iraq, on Nov. 4, 2004, when a roadside bomb struck his patrol. The two deaths left parents Jeff and Peggy Hubbard mourning two of their three sons.

The family’s surviving son, Jason Hubbard, had served in Iraq with Jared and later returned to the war as Nathan deployed. Jason was still in Iraq when Nathan’s helicopter went down. His unit was involved in securing the crash area and recovering the dead, placing him at the scene where his youngest brother’s remains were found.

Jason did not initially know that Nathan was aboard the aircraft. He learned during the recovery operation that his brother had been one of the soldiers on the helicopter, turning what began as another military assignment into an intensely personal ordeal. He witnessed the recovery and identification process before accompanying Nathan home.

The circumstances underscored the Hubbard family’s extraordinary involvement in the Iraq war. Jared and Jason had enlisted before Nathan. After Jared’s death, Nathan continued with his own plans to serve, joining the Army and eventually deploying with the 2nd Battalion, 35th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Brigade Combat Team, 25th Infantry Division, based at Schofield Barracks, Hawaii.

At the funeral, Nathan was remembered not only as a soldier but as a son and brother whose decision to serve had been shaped by loyalty to his family and fellow troops. His death came less than three years after Jared’s, forcing the family and the wider Clovis community to repeat the rituals of military mourning.

Jason, standing with his parents at the second funeral, represented both the family’s long connection to the Army and the burden carried by those who return. After Nathan’s death, the Army removed Jason from Iraq under policies intended to prevent a family from losing its last surviving son in combat.

The service ended with the presentation of the folded American flag to Nathan’s family. His burial beside Jared left two neighboring graves as a stark record of one family’s sacrifice — and of a surviving brother who had served with one fallen sibling and helped bring the other home.
